title: Scaffolding
text:
How does an adult best help a child learn something the child cannot yet do alone? In the early 1970s, David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross studied this question with a puzzle and a careful tutor.

The puzzle was a set of interlocking wooden blocks that could be assembled into a pyramid, a task well beyond most three-year-olds and challenging for five-year-olds. Gail Ross worked one on one with children aged three, four and five. Her approach was deliberate. She first let the child try alone. When the child got stuck, she offered a spoken hint. If that did not work, she showed how to put two pieces together, then handed the task back. When the child succeeded at a step, she stepped back again.

Watching the sessions, the researchers identified what the tutor was doing. She kept the child interested, simplified the task by handling parts the child could not yet manage, kept the child pointed toward the goal, highlighted the important features, controlled frustration, and modeled solutions. They called this support scaffolding: a temporary structure that holds things up while building goes on and is removed as the child takes over.

The term spread widely through education and parenting, where it is still used to describe good teaching.
lesson: When helping someone learn, give just enough support to keep them moving, then step back as they gain control. Doing it for them teaches little.
people: David Wood, Jerome Bruner, Gail Ross
source: Wood, D., Bruner, J. S., and Ross, G. (1976). The role of tutoring in problem solving. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2), 89-100.
